newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria defends its human rights record.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria defends its human rights record.

text.p: Nigeria's military government dismissed international criticism on Monday and told a visiting African mission it had an excellent human rights record.

"In comparism to other parts of the world, particularly the developed countries, Nigeria's record on human rights is good if not better," government chief secretary Gidado Idris told an African mission that arrived at the weekend to promote respect for human rights in the West African country.
Local rights activists say the team from the Gambia-based African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, an Organisation of African Unity agency, is not objective. Some decided not to meet it.
It is led by the Ghanaian deputy chairman of the commission Professor Victor Danqua. Others are former Togolese minister Koffi Amega and Essombe Joseph, a lawyer with the agency.
Danqua said the team came with an open mind to enquire about the rights situation in Nigeria.

It has met officials overseeing the military government's transition to democracy and visited the cities of Kaduna and Kano in the north and is expected to head to Lagos on Tuesday to meet opposition groups.

Two weeks ago two United Nations investigators called off a similar mission after authorities denied them access to jails and political detainees, including presidential claimant Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of a 1993 annulled vote.

Local rights activists say the government is using the African team to counter the effects of the U.N. mission. Nigeria is expected to be in the dock at the six-week session of the U.N. Human Rights Commission which opened in Geneva on Monday.

A Nigerian court on Monday ordered the military government to free a pro-democracy activist detained since December, witnesses said. Security authorities said he was being held for a series of bombings that have rocked Lagos.

It was the second time the Lagos high court had ordered the release of Frederick Fasehun, chairman of the Campaign for Democracy. Government lawyers objected to the release order in January but Justice Mutiu Bioshogun said they had not shown enough cause for him to rescind his order.
Nigerian police have blamed the umbrella opposition group NADECO (National Democratic Coalition) for the bombings. NADECO denies any involvement.
